items.title: Maria Schneider interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001
items.q: Her innovative writing for jazz ensembles has won great critical praise... gained valuable experience in her associations with Bob Brookmeyer and Gil Evans.

ctx.x: I can hear it in your pieces. And I was interested to hear the other night that your pieces don’t seem to usually start with one groove and keep in all the way. That they have sections and things happen to the time and things happen to the emotion within them.

Yeah. You know it’s something I started to realize about jazz, because I have to say I’m really disappointed in a lot of jazz I hear — not that I listen and say I’m disappointed — but I just lose interest pretty quickly. And I think that jazz at one time was music that, it just evolved. Later it was named jazz, and then everybody goes back and analyzes how it © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

came into being or whatever. But it was something that came up spontaneously from something very deep and cultural and human and personal and sociological, everything came together. And for me now, what happens is when people, say they’re writing music, they have this template of how music has been behind them. Like okay it’s jazz. That means it has a rhythm section, probably drumset, it means that there’s a bass line, it means that there is something comping, it means that there is a solo section, it means that…
